title: Spec Kit: Spec-Driven Development with AI Agents
description: What Spec Kit solves, core terminology, sample prompts, and drawbacks — especially weak product-level memory — with practical workarounds.

blocks.content: [Spec Kit](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/) (often called **Speckit**) is GitHub’s open-source harness for **Spec-Driven Development (SDD)**. Instead of dumping a vague prompt into an AI coding agent and hoping for the best, you walk the agent through structured phases — each producing Markdown artifacts that feed the next.

blocks.text: Describe *what* to build and refine it through structured phases. Keep intent at the center; let the agent handle implementation detail.

blocks.body: Core loop: **Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement**, with optional quality gates (**clarify**, **checklist**, **analyze**) and a final **converge** check. In Cursor, these usually appear as skills like `speckit-specify`; docs often show `/speckit.specify` — same steps, different invocation form.

blocks.content: The problem it solves
AI agents are strong at generating code and weak at holding a durable product intent. Ad-hoc chats tend to:

items: **Skip the product conversation** — jump to frameworks and file trees before outcomes are clear
**Lose decisions** — clarifications live in chat history, not in a reviewable artifact
**Drift across files** — implementation diverges from what you thought you asked for
**Skip review gates** — large features ship without a consistent checklist against the original ask

blocks.content: Spec Kit fixes that by making **intent artifacts first-class**. You write (or generate) a feature spec, clarify ambiguity, lock a technical plan, break work into dependency-ordered tasks, then implement — and finally check the codebase against those artifacts. Humans stay in the loop at review gates; the agent gets structured context instead of a one-shot prompt.

blocks.body: Use the **short path** for small features (`specify → plan → tasks → implement → converge`). Use the **full path** when ambiguity or production risk is high — add constitution, clarify, checklist, and analyze.

blocks.content: Main terminologies

items: **Spec-Driven Development (SDD)** — build by refining intent artifacts before (and during) coding
**Constitution** — project-wide principles and constraints every later step is checked against (lives in `.specify/memory/constitution.md`)
**Feature directory** — one folder under `specs/` (e.g. `specs/001-content-page-foundation/`) holding that feature’s artifacts
**Active feature** — which feature Spec Kit commands target; tracked in `.specify/feature.json` (not solely by git branch)
**spec.md** — user-facing *what* and *why*: user stories, acceptance scenarios, out-of-scope
**plan.md** — *how*: tech stack, architecture, constitution check, project structure
**Design artifacts** — usually `research.md`, `data-model.md`, `contracts/`, `quickstart.md` produced during planning
**tasks.md** — dependency-ordered, phase-grouped work items the implement step executes
**Checklist** — “unit tests for English”: validates requirement quality, not runtime behavior
**Review gate** — human approve/reject pause between phases (e.g. before planning or tasking)
**Integration** — the coding agent adapter (Cursor, Copilot, Claude, Gemini, …) Spec Kit was initialized with
**Extension / hook** — optional plugins that run before/after commands (e.g. auto-create a git feature branch)
**Converge** — gap analysis of code vs spec/plan/tasks; appends missing tasks until the feature is complete

blocks.content: The workflow at a glance

items: **Constitution** — set ground rules (once per project, update when principles change)
**Specify** — describe the feature in product language
**Clarify** — resolve underspecified decisions (before planning)
**Plan** — choose stack and produce design artifacts
**Checklist** — stress-test the requirements for clarity and coverage
**Tasks** — break the plan into ordered, testable work
**Analyze** — cross-check spec, plan, and tasks for conflicts
**Implement** — execute tasks in dependency order
**Converge** — find leftover gaps; implement again until converged

blocks.content: Sample prompts for each step

Examples below use `/speckit.*` as in the official docs. In Cursor, invoke the matching skill (e.g. `speckit-specify`) and pass the same argument text. Prompts are illustrative — adapt names and constraints to your project.

sections.title: Tip: Generate a constitution prompt from ChatGPT
sections.body:
Drop the following prompt into ChatGPT to generate a proper prompt for constitution.

```text
I am building a frontend application using react.

Help me create a GitHub Spec Kit /speckit.constitution prompt for this project.

Before writing it:
- Review the latest GitHub Spec Kit documentation to understand the purpose of the /speckit.constitution command and what belongs in a project constitution.
- Review the latest react documentation and accepted best practices for developing frontend applications with react.
- Ask me questions to understand my project, coding standards, architecture preferences, testing strategy, UI technology, persistence layer, and team conventions.

After you have enough information:
- Create a complete /speckit.constitution prompt.
- Include only long-term project rules that should apply to every feature.
- Do not include feature-specific requirements.
- Briefly explain why you included each rule.
```

blocks.content: 1. Constitution
Establish principles the agent must honor on every feature.

blocks.code: /speckit.constitution Randomism is a JSON-driven blog. Content lives in versioned article JSON; app code only loads and renders via a single component registry. Spec-first delivery is mandatory. Prefer static generation, no CMS or auth. Keep the public UI simple and mobile-usable.

blocks.content: 2. Specify
Focus on **what** and **why** — not frameworks. Name users, outcomes, and hard exclusions.

blocks.code: /speckit.specify Build a content page foundation: a site that loads in-repo JSON articles, validates them against a documented block schema, renders blocks through one component registry, and ships a home article list plus sample articles with title/description/Open Graph metadata. Include Heading, Paragraph, and Image blocks. No CMS, backend, auth, or tests in this phase.

blocks.content: 3. Clarify
Ask the agent to surface up to a handful of high-impact ambiguities and fold answers back into `spec.md`. Optionally focus a domain.

blocks.code: /speckit.clarify Focus on publishing rules — draft vs published visibility, slug derivation from filenames, and what happens when article JSON fails schema validation at build time.

blocks.content: 4. Plan
This is where stack and architecture belong. Be explicit about libraries, folders, and constraints.

blocks.code: /speckit.plan Use Next.js App Router with TypeScript. Articles live under data/articles/*.json. Validate with Zod (or equivalent) against a documented block union. Render via a single component registry. Prefer static generation for public routes. Keep styling minimal and mobile-first.

blocks.content: 5. Checklist
Generate “unit tests for English” — completeness, clarity, consistency, edge cases — not runtime test cases.

blocks.code: /speckit.checklist Focus on content schema clarity: are all block types, required fields, draft/publish rules, and SEO metadata requirements unambiguous and consistent?

blocks.content: 6. Tasks
Usually needs little argument — it reads plan + spec and emits phased `tasks.md`.

blocks.body: Optional nudge: `/speckit.tasks Prefer small independently testable tasks per user story; mark parallel-safe work clearly.`

blocks.content: 7. Analyze
Read-only consistency pass across `spec.md`, `plan.md`, and `tasks.md`. Fix source artifacts, then re-run before implementing.
8. Implement
Execute `tasks.md` in order. For large features, scope a phase so context stays manageable.

blocks.code:
/speckit.implement

# Or scoped:
/speckit.implement Implement only Setup and Foundational phases: project scaffolding, article loader, schema validation, and registry. Stop before user-story UI polish.

blocks.content: 9. Converge
Compare the codebase to the artifacts. Missing work is appended to `tasks.md` — run implement again until the feature reports converged.
After implement: improve what’s left

Finishing `/speckit.implement` once does not mean the feature is done. Agents often mark tasks complete while leaving gaps — partial acceptance criteria, skipped edge cases, plan decisions not wired through, or constitution MUST rules only half-honored.

blocks.body: When you review the result and see “more that should be there,” **do not open a free-form chat to patch it.** Put the missing work back into the Spec Kit loop.
**Implement finishes tasks. Converge finds what’s still missing.** Treat “looks incomplete” as a signal to converge, not as a reason to abandon the artifacts.

blocks.content: The improve loop

items: **Review the ship** — run the app, skim the diff, and check user stories / acceptance scenarios against what actually landed

**Clarify related but undefined intent** — if the improvement belongs to this feature but was never written into `spec.md`, run `/speckit.clarify` (scoped to that gap) so the requirement lands in the spec before you chase code; re-run plan/tasks only if architecture or task breakdown must change

**Run converge** — when the intent is already in the artifacts, `/speckit.converge` compares the codebase to `spec.md`, `plan.md`, and `tasks.md` (plus the constitution) and appends a new Convergence phase of tasks for every remaining gap
**Implement the appended tasks** — `/speckit.implement` again, optionally scoped to the Convergence phase (or to tasks added after clarify/plan/tasks)
**Re-converge** — repeat until converge reports no remaining gaps

blocks.code:
# Related improvement not yet in the spec after initial implement:
/speckit.clarify Focus on empty and error states for the home article list — fold decisions into spec.md.

# Gaps against intent already in the artifacts:
/speckit.converge

# After tasks are appended:
/speckit.implement Implement only the latest Convergence phase.

# Then check again:
/speckit.converge

blocks.content: What converge catches (and what it doesn’t)

Converge is gap analysis against **stated intent**, not a general code-quality review. It classifies leftovers as missing, partial, contradicts, or unrequested — then turns actionable findings into checklist items in `tasks.md`. It does **not** rewrite the spec or plan, and it does **not** invent product requirements you never wrote down.

items: **Use converge when** — implement “finished” but acceptance scenarios fail, planned files/behaviors are thin or absent, or constitution MUST rules are violated

**Update the artifacts first when** — you want *better* behavior that was never specified (new edge case, stricter UX, extra polish). Add it to `spec.md` (and plan/tasks if needed), then implement — or let converge pick it up only after the intent exists on disk
**Stay in the loop** — review the Convergence findings table before the next implement run; drop or rephrase tasks that are noise

blocks.body: If quality gaps keep reappearing after converge reports clean, the intent was too thin — tighten `spec.md` / `plan.md`, regenerate or extend tasks, then implement. Converge cannot enforce standards that never made it into the artifacts.

blocks.content: Drawbacks and workarounds

Spec Kit is strong at **shipping a feature end-to-end**. It is weaker at keeping a durable **big-picture map of the whole app**. Feature folders under `specs/` answer “what is this change?”; they rarely answer “how does the product fit together?” Treat the gaps below as design trade-offs, not bugs — and pair Spec Kit with a thin layer of system docs.

blocks.body: **Feature memory ≠ product memory.** A polished `spec.md` / `plan.md` / `tasks.md` trio can still leave newcomers (and future agent sessions) without a shared picture of domains, routes, data ownership, or how features relate.

blocks.content: Weak product-level / big-picture memory

Artifacts are scoped per feature. Cross-cutting concerns — domain map, primary user journeys, module boundaries, “source of truth” for content vs code — either live only in the constitution (too high-level) or get reinvented in each plan (too local).

items: **Workaround: keep a short system overview** — a living `docs/project-overview.md` (or ADR folder) that lists domains, key routes, data stores, and invariants in a few pages
**Workaround: point agents at docs folder — in plan/implement prompts, require reading the overview + active feature dir, not only `spec.md`

blocks.content: Knowledge stays siloed in feature directories
After many features, useful decisions are scattered across dozens of `research.md` / `data-model.md` files. Discoverability drops; agents and humans both re-ask settled questions.

items: **Workaround: promote durable decisions** — when a research note becomes product-wide, copy a short summary into the architecture doc or an ADR; leave the feature file as history
**Workaround: tag ownership in the feature index** — e.g. “block schema → `002-blog-block-catalog`” so later work knows where the contract lives
**Workaround: converge with a doc task** — after implement, add an explicit task to update the overview when routes, schemas, or boundaries changed

blocks.content: Constitution is principles, not a map
The constitution is excellent for governance (“spec-first”, “content–code separation”) and poor as an encyclopedia. Stuffing the whole app model into it bloats context and still goes stale.

items: **Workaround: two layers** — constitution = rules; architecture/ADRs = structure and history
**Workaround: keep constitution executable** — prefer short, checkable constraints over narrative product essays
**Workaround: version and prune** — when principles change, update constitution deliberately; move outdated product detail out to docs

blocks.content: Process overhead and context pressure
Full-path SDD generates a lot of Markdown. Review burden rises; long implement runs can push constitution and overview out of the agent’s active context, so rules get “forgotten” mid-flight.

items: **Workaround: choose path by risk** — short path for small changes; full path when ambiguity or production impact is high
**Workaround: scope implement** — one phase (or one user story) per run; re-read constitution + overview at the start of each run
**Workaround: distill always-on rules** — Cursor rules / agent skills that echo the few constraints that must never drift

blocks.content: Brownfield and cross-feature refactors

Spec Kit shines on greenfield features with a crisp boundary. Large existing codebases and “change everything that touches X” refactors are harder: there is no automatic inventory of the current system, and feature specs do not replace exploration.

items: **Workaround: document-as-you-go** — first feature (or a dedicated “baseline” spec) captures current architecture before net-new work
**Workaround: spike outside Spec Kit, then specify** — explore the codebase, write findings into the overview, then run specify/plan on the delta
**Workaround: slice by seam** — one Spec Kit feature per bounded change; use the feature index to sequence dependent slices

blocks.body: **Practical combo:** Spec Kit for *feature delivery*; a thin architecture doc + feature index for *product memory*; constitution for *non-negotiable rules*. None of the three alone is enough.

blocks.content: Practical tips

items: **Separate what from how** — keep stack talk out of specify; put it in plan
**Review the Markdown** — treat `spec.md` / `plan.md` / `tasks.md` like PRs; gates exist for a reason
**Clarify early** — ambiguity after plan usually means expensive rework
**Scope implement** — phase-sized runs beat one giant agent session for big features
**Re-converge** — “done” means converge reports no remaining gaps, not that implement finished once
**Update the big picture** — when a feature changes routes, schemas, or boundaries, refresh the architecture overview in the same PR

blocks.body: Skipping clarify/analyze on fuzzy product work often produces a clean-looking `tasks.md` that encodes the wrong product. Prefer a short clarification session over a long cleanup PR.

blocks.content: When an agent session starts feeling like guesswork, step back to the artifact that should already answer the question — overview for product shape, spec for behavior, plan for stack, tasks for sequencing — and update that file before asking for more code.
